home.name: Adam Acovski
home.intro: Hydrogeologist and data engineer in Denver. I build calibrated groundwater models with rigorous uncertainty quantification, and the pipelines, APIs, and dashboards that put their results in front of the people making decisions.

resume.summary: Data scientist and data engineer with nearly a decade of predictive modeling experience, specializing in Python/SQL and scalable data pipelines for environmental and groundwater problems. Builds calibrated predictive models with rigorous uncertainty quantification (PEST++, iterative ensemble smoothers) and the production systems behind them: ETL pipelines, lakehouse storage, APIs, cloud infrastructure, and CI/CD. Domain depth from mining and environmental consulting, including groundwater flow and contaminant transport modeling, dewatering assessments, and model calibration.

experience.title: Consultant (Hydrogeology)
bullets: Develop conceptual and numerical groundwater models that predict mine-site flow conditions for engineering decisions
Work with exploration data in Leapfrog to inform conceptual hydrogeological models
QA/QC geochemistry data for errors, gaps, and inconsistencies before use in analysis and reporting

Design ETL pipelines on DuckDB and DuckLake that store monitoring, field, and model-output time series in normalized tables keyed by sensor and timestamp, with analysis-ready views for modeling and reporting
Transform raw sensor data in-database, such as converting vibrating wire piezometer readings into water levels, so derived values stay traceable to source readings
Serve analytical results to project teams through FastAPI services and React front ends, containerized with Docker on VPN-accessible servers
Maintain CI/CD pipelines with automated testing for analytical code and deployments

experience.title: Project Hydrogeologist

Provisioned infrastructure as code with Pulumi and Docker, with CI/CD through GitHub Actions and Cloud Build and documentation published to AWS S3; unit tests guarded modeling scripts against regressions during refactoring
